claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based plasma-facing components is governed by grain-boundary mobility.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based plasma-facing components is governed by grain-boundary mobility.
Rhenium added to tungsten preferentially segregates to grain boundaries.
Rhenium segregation strengthens tungsten grain boundaries.
Solute-segregated grain boundaries resist grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature operation.
Hindering grain-boundary sliding reduces the rate of high-temperature plastic deformation.
The reduction in high-temperature plastic-deformation rate caused by inhibited grain-boundary sliding improves toughness.
Doped tungsten will have a lower high-temperature creep rate than an otherwise comparable undoped baseline.
Doped tungsten will have greater high-temperature fracture toughness than an otherwise comparable undoped baseline.
The proposed effect should hold above approximately 1000 °C under sustained mechanical loading in an inert or controlled atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism should apply to tungsten-based and similar refractory plasma-facing materials with comparable grain sizes and processing histories.
Changes in material system or processing parameters may limit the applicability of the proposed mechanism.
The magnitude of creep-rate and toughness changes depends on dopant concentration, dopant-distribution uniformity, and thermal-mechanical history.
TEM and atom-probe tomography can confirm dopant segregation at tungsten grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary cohesion can be determined through the proposed TEM/APT characterization.
